assumptions.summary: Local interests are operationalized as financial profit only.
People attracted by wildlife are operationalized as tourists.
Policy effects are treated as separable enough for component scoring.
Criteria are treated as sufficiently independent for the network and AHP construction.
Fitted trends are used as proxies for wildlife and resource response.
Pairwise judgments are treated as acceptable when the consistency ratio passes the source threshold.
Policy alternatives are compared under a common objective across zones.
Sensitivity is interpreted only over displayed parameter perturbations.
Transfer checks are limited by sparse and nonannual observations.

context_sources.observation: The Summary addresses four official tasks: area policies, ranking, long-term trends and transfer, and a two-page committee report.
The source divides the reserve into 36 equal 50 km2 grids and selects among wildlife, hunting, tourism, and agriculture uses.
The paper maximizes ecological benefit and economic benefit separately and reports three Lingo scenarios rather than one optimum.
Dijkstra is applied to an undirected four-zone graph with pairwise weights and environmental, climatic, and population terms.
The paper reports a quadratic tourism-revenue fit with R-squared 0.926 and uses a one-percent visitor-growth assumption.
A three-versus-three pre/post COVID-19 t-test reports t=4.354 and p=0.049.
Yellowstone adaptation changes resident-income and visitor-cap constraints, then names five destination districts.
Four special events perturb weights by at most 0.1 and the paper reports Scenario 2 as largest in each case.

contributions.summary: Uses an ordinal Summary to connect six official requirements to a network score, policy scenarios, testing, and a committee report.
Moves from ordinary wildlife value and community pressure to an explicit six-part requirement inventory.
Decomposes the evaluation into wildlife, resources, finance, tourism, and a final objective.
Uses AHP comparisons and consistency checks before applying the common score to area-specific policy sets.
Reports separate rankings for core wildlife, settlement, and grazing zones.
Perturbs weights and interactions to qualify rank stability.
Tests fitted trends and climate-transfer behavior while preserving sparse-data limits.
Restates policy implications and unresolved transfer boundaries.
Translates the technical ranking into a two-page nontechnical committee memo with budget-limited choices.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Background and literature sources motivate wildlife, community, tourism, and policy interactions.
The nomenclature table names policy, species, resource, score, and AHP quantities but leaves some units and index domains implicit.
Wildlife trajectories and protection values are fitted from source-selected observations.
Pasture, livestock density, and water-stress inputs are converted to a resource score.
Local financial interest is built from agricultural, livestock, employment, and cost proxies.
Tourists are used as a proxy for people attracted by wildlife.
AHP matrices provide pairwise judgments and consistency quantities.
Policy tables define alternatives for core, settlement, and grazing zones.
Testing uses sparse, nonannual, selected survey, and climate-transfer observations.
References provide external provenance but not a complete input checksum ledger.

independent_extensions.summary: Replace financial-only local interest with a multi-attribute community utility and stakeholder elicitation.
Add species-specific observation models and causal poaching-policy identification.
Propagate AHP judgment uncertainty into policy-rank intervals.
Use annual panel data and climate scenarios for transfer validation.
Build a reconciled committee claim register with owners, triggers, monitoring, and rollback.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: A judge may value the ordinal Summary because it makes six requirements scannable before technical detail.
A judge may value the five-component decomposition while requiring proxy, unit, and causal boundaries.
A judge may value visible AHP consistency checks while asking for stakeholder elicitation and rank stability.
A judge may value area-specific rankings while rejecting universal policy claims from one internal score.
A judge may value the committee report's concrete choices while requiring reconciled numbers, owners, triggers, and transfer limits.

source.title: Build a common paradise for humans and wildlife in the Maasai Mara

source_quality.summary: Text and visual coverage are complete, but exact data, proxy definitions, causal fits, AHP judgments, rankings, transfer tests, reproducibility, uncertainty, and independent validation remain incomplete.

task_reconstruction: Develop area-specific wildlife, settlement, and grazing policies.
Construct a methodology and ranking with interaction and economic models.
Analyze long-term trends, certainty, and transferability.
Write a two-page nontechnical committee report with policy choices and budget constraints.

unresolved_questions.summary: The paper does not provide a requirement-by-requirement map from the official Maasai Mara prompt to each claimed result.
The 36 equal 50 km2 cells assume uniform environmental and economic conditions within each cell, which can distort boundary decisions.
Animal weights are illustrative and include a negative antelope weight, but no elicitation, calibration, or sensitivity record is supplied.
The source lists URLs and references but does not freeze retrieval dates, downloaded files, transformations, or checksums.
Several extracted symbols are unreadable or inconsistent, so variable identity and inequality direction need original-PDF reconciliation.
Xj is described both as an i-species conservation decision and as a j-area use, leaving its index domain ambiguous.
The source combines about 410 daily visitors with 40 visitors per tourist area without a reconciled occupancy derivation.
The reported ecological value and economic values mix unit-area, annual, million-dollar, and per-capita quantities without one dimensional ledger.
The paper says there is no optimum and supplies three scenarios, but does not specify a Pareto rule or decision-maker preference.
The reserve is reduced to an undirected graph with equal grid-edge lengths and hand-set pairwise weights, not measured movement paths.
Coefficients b1-b3 and environmental, climate, and population inputs are not estimated or reproduced.
Scenario economic values are reported as very large totals without a dated currency basis, area multiplier, or reconciled arithmetic.
The quadratic fit and linear comparator lack raw regression rows, coefficient uncertainty, residual diagnostics, and a reproducible script.
The assumed one-percent annual visitor increase is not identified from policy evidence and is applied beyond the observed period.
The pandemic t-test uses only three observations per group and does not state test assumptions, variance choice, or multiple-comparison handling.
The claim that shorter agricultural-wildlife distance reduces losses is not supported by an estimated attack or crop-loss model.
The Yellowstone table prints an establishment date inconsistent with the commonly cited founding year, and the discrepancy is not discussed.
The Yellowstone migration changes two constraints but does not validate the adapted rankings or quantify transfer uncertainty.
The Yellowstone visitor total and daily-cap calculation are not reconciled with the 40-person-per-tourist-area assumption.
The nontechnical report recommends actions but provides no cost envelope, responsible owner, trigger, monitoring metric, or rollback rule.
The four special-event weight changes are selected by hand and do not establish global robustness or rank-reversal probability.
The sensitivity table's economic values are not dimensionally reconciled with the baseline scenario values.
The conclusion calls the model stable from R-squared values above 0.8, which is not a sufficient validation criterion for policy ranking.
References identify external studies and websites but do not provide exact source snapshots or geographic filters.
The appendix names MATLAB, Python, and Lingo but omits a complete executable model, inputs, solver settings, and expected outputs.
The Dijkstra code is truncated at the page boundary and cannot by itself reproduce the reported zoning result.
Balancing residents is operationalized mainly as per-capita income and profit allocation, omitting land rights, culture, safety, and distribution.
The no-major-disaster assumption excludes shocks that can materially change conservation, tourism, and agricultural outcomes.
Immediate and complete implementation is assumed without enforcement capacity, delay, behavioral response, or budget constraints.
Summary, body, tables, and appendix contain typographical and numerical inconsistencies that require a final claim register.

writing_logic.summary: Summary: Maasai Mara wildlife, residents, four land uses, four official requirements, and a committee decision -> advance through repeated task-method-result rungs -> pair dual-goal planning, Dijkstra interaction, economic comparison, forecasts, transfer, sensitivity, and report advice -> a scan-ready answer ladder -> 1.Introduction.

Committee report: the Kenyan committee's resource plan, recommendations, and implementation cautions -> state the proposed arrangement first, then list concrete policy actions -> translate the grid plan, ecological value, and human-wildlife balance into direct public prose -> a committee-facing policy memo -> 9. Sensitivity analysis of the model.

1.1 Background: wildlife value, Kenyan tourism, residents, and resource protection -> move from a familiar reserve to the government's balancing problem -> connect wildlife, tourism finance, local livelihoods, and zoning -> a bounded conservation motivation -> 1.2 Restatement of the problem.

1.2 Restatement of the problem: four official tasks: area policy, ranking, long-term outcomes, and a committee report -> translate the prompt into an ordered checklist -> separate policy design, interaction and economic comparison, trend certainty, transfer, and communication -> an answerable requirement inventory -> 1.3 Literature review.

1.3 Literature review: reserve zoning, ecotourism, community livelihoods, wildlife populations, and network selection -> locate the contribution after a short literature handoff -> justify combining ecological, economic, distance, and policy views -> a contribution gap -> 1.4 Our work.

1.4 Our work: data cleaning, dual-goal planning, Dijkstra, regression, migration, and report writing -> preview the workflow before formal assumptions -> order data, model construction, solution, prediction, extension, and communication -> a visible end-to-end workflow -> 2.Assumption and Justification.

2.Assumption and Justification: reliable data, no major disasters, bounded influences, uniform grid cells, and Kenya proxies -> state each premise and attach its justification immediately -> make the zoning, income, tourist, and transfer boundaries explicit -> a conditional modeling envelope -> 3.Notations and Definitions.

3.1 Notations: area decisions, ecological value, power, population, interaction, and program indicators -> freeze a compact symbol vocabulary -> type the quantities consumed by ecological and economic constraints -> a partial notation ledger -> 3.2 Definitions.

3.2 Definitions: resources, lost opportunities, attracted people, and negative interactions -> define ambiguous prompt language before modeling -> separate residents, tourists, wildlife, and conflict categories -> an operational definition ledger -> 4.Data.

4.Data: animal, terrain, climate, hydrology, economic, and living-standard data -> move from data collection to screening and visualization -> separate cited databases from the paper's transformations and values -> a source-data inventory -> 5.Problem 1.

5.1 Problem analysis: area policies that conserve resources while balancing residents -> state the zoning objective before formulas -> motivate dual-goal planning and constraints -> a problem-specific model brief -> 5.2 Preparation of the model.

5.2 Preparation of the model: tourism revenue, agricultural and hunting output, normalized vegetation and wildlife -> define economic quantities before ecological quantities -> turn heterogeneous inputs into comparable ecological and economic benefits -> typed benefit components -> 5.3 Establishment of the model.

5.3 Establishment of the model: 36 grid cells, binary land-use decisions, ecological bands, tourists, and residents -> build decisions and constraints in numbered steps -> connect wildlife distribution to area use, capacity, income, and dual objectives -> a constrained resource allocation model -> 5.4 Solution of the model.

5.4 Solution of the model: three Lingo scenarios with different counts of four area types -> present the solver outcome after the constraints -> compare scenario counts without claiming a unique optimum -> three candidate zoning plans -> 6.Problem 2.

6.1 Problem analysis: human-animal interaction and economic outcomes for the three plans -> state the comparison criterion before the graph -> combine negative interaction and economic benefit -> a policy-ranking objective -> 6.2 Minimum interaction model.

6.2 Minimum interaction model: four interaction types, an undirected graph, pairwise weights, and Dijkstra -> define each interaction and then give the algorithm -> use shortest paths as a distance-based proxy for conflict -> a minimum-interaction comparison -> 6.3 Economic impact evaluation model.

6.3 Economic impact evaluation model: ecological value and economic value for each zoning scenario -> put the scenario table before the decision sentence -> compare economic totals with interaction results to select Scenario 2 -> a combined policy ranking -> 7.Problem 3.

7.1 Problem analysis: policy changes, tourism, agriculture, COVID-19, national economy, and transfer -> state the long-term questions before fitting data -> separate trend, shock, feedback, and migration questions -> a forecast and transfer brief -> 7.2 Long-term development.

7.2 Long-term development: tourism revenue, agriculture, COVID-19, and a virtuous economic-conservation cycle -> move from fitted baseline to shock test and policy feedback -> use a quadratic regression, visitor growth, a t-test, and a causal narrative -> bounded long-term predictions -> 7.3 Model Migration.

7.3 Model Migration: Yellowstone similarities, wildlife and terrain maps, income, visitor capacity, and five districts -> compare reserves before changing constraints -> adapt income and capacity constraints while retaining transfer caveats -> a destination-reserve extension -> 8.Problem 4.

8.Problem 4: a two-page nontechnical plan, four land uses, and four balancing recommendations -> state the plan in plain language and then list actions -> translate model output into community cooperation, visitor safety, regulation, and livelihood balance -> a committee-facing recommendation -> 9. Sensitivity analysis of the model.

9.Sensitivity analysis: food crisis, natural disaster, policy change, financial crisis, and weight perturbations -> vary one special case at a time after the baseline ranking -> read economic values and goodness of fit as local stability evidence -> a bounded sensitivity claim -> 10.Evaluation and extension.

10.Evaluation and extension: scalability, visualization, time dimension, data proxies, and Yellowstone extension -> group strengths before naming limitations -> separate communication advantages from proxy, data, and transfer weaknesses -> a repair-oriented evaluation -> 11.Reference.

11.Reference: wildlife, tourism, population, zoning, and Kenyan-law sources -> record external provenance after conclusions -> separate references from paper-created transformations and rankings -> a partial source ledger -> 12.Appendix.

12.Appendix: software, industry data, and a Dijkstra MATLAB function -> close with data and implementation material -> retain the source's reproducibility evidence and its truncation boundary -> an appendix evidence record -> Independent replay.
